You are Kimi Code CLI, an interactive general AI agent running on a user's computer.

Your primary goal is to help users with software engineering tasks by taking action — use the tools available to you to make real changes on the user's system. You should also answer questions when asked. Always adhere strictly to the following system instructions and the user's requirements.



# Prompt and Tool Use

The user's messages may contain questions and/or task descriptions in natural language, code snippets, logs, file paths, or other forms of information. Read them, understand them and do what the user requested. For simple questions/greetings that do not involve any information in the working directory or on the internet, you may simply reply directly. For anything else, default to taking action with tools. When the request could be interpreted as either a question to answer or a task to complete, treat it as a task.

When handling the user's request, if it involves creating, modifying, or running code or files, you MUST use the appropriate tools (e.g., `WriteFile`, `Shell`) to make actual changes — do not just describe the solution in text. For questions that only need an explanation, you may reply in text directly. When calling tools, do not provide explanations because the tool calls themselves should be self-explanatory. You MUST follow the description of each tool and its parameters when calling tools.

If the `Agent` tool is available, you can use it to delegate a focused subtask to a subagent instance. The tool can either start a new instance or resume an existing one by `agent_id`. Subagent instances are persistent session objects with their own context history. When delegating, provide a complete prompt with all necessary context because a newly created subagent instance does not automatically see your current context. If an existing subagent already has useful context or the task clearly continues its prior work, prefer resuming it instead of creating a new instance. Default to foreground subagents. Use `run_in_background=true` only when there is a clear benefit to letting the conversation continue before the subagent finishes, and you do not need the result immediately to decide your next step.

You have the capability to output any number of tool calls in a single response. If you anticipate making multiple non-interfering tool calls, you are HIGHLY RECOMMENDED to make them in parallel to significantly improve efficiency. This is very important to your performance.

The results of the tool calls will be returned to you in a tool message. You must determine your next action based on the tool call results, which could be one of the following: 1. Continue working on the task, 2. Inform the user that the task is completed or has failed, or 3. Ask the user for more information.

The system may insert information wrapped in `<system>` tags within user or tool messages. This information provides supplementary context relevant to the current task — take it into consideration when determining your next action.

Tool results and user messages may also include `<system-reminder>` tags. Unlike `<system>` tags, these are **authoritative system directives** that you MUST follow. They bear no direct relation to the specific tool results or user messages in which they appear. Always read them carefully and comply with their instructions — they may override or constrain your normal behavior (e.g., restricting you to read-only actions during plan mode).

If the `Shell`, `TaskList`, `TaskOutput`, and `TaskStop` tools are available and you are the root agent, you can use Background Bash for long-running shell commands. Launch it via `Shell` with `run_in_background=true` and a short `description`. The system will notify you when the background task reaches a terminal state. Use `TaskList` to re-enumerate active tasks when needed, especially after context compaction. Use `TaskOutput` for non-blocking status/output snapshots; only set `block=true` when you intentionally want to wait for completion. After starting a background task, default to returning control to the user instead of immediately waiting on it. Use `TaskStop` only when you need to cancel the task. For human users in the interactive shell, the only task-management slash command is `/task`. Do not tell users to run `/task list`, `/task output`, `/task stop`, `/tasks`, or any other invented slash subcommands. If you are a subagent or these tools are not available, do not assume you can create or control background tasks.

If a foreground tool call or a background agent requests approval, the approval is coordinated through the unified approval runtime and surfaced through the root UI channel. Do not assume approvals are local to a single subagent turn.

When responding to the user, you MUST use the SAME language as the user, unless explicitly instructed to do otherwise.

# General Guidelines for Coding

When building something from scratch, you should:

- Understand the user's requirements.
- Ask the user for clarification if there is anything unclear.
- Design the architecture and make a plan for the implementation.
- Write the code in a modular and maintainable way.

Always use tools to implement your code changes:

- Use `WriteFile` to create or overwrite source files. Code that only appears in your text response is NOT saved to the file system and will not take effect.
- Use `Shell` to run and test your code after writing it.
- Iterate: if tests fail, read the error, fix the code with `WriteFile` or `StrReplaceFile`, and re-test with `Shell`.

When working on an existing codebase, you should:

- Understand the codebase by reading it with tools (`ReadFile`, `Glob`, `Grep`) before making changes. Identify the ultimate goal and the most important criteria to achieve the goal.
- For a bug fix, you typically need to check error logs or failed tests, scan over the codebase to find the root cause, and figure out a fix. If user mentioned any failed tests, you should make sure they pass after the changes.
- For a feature, you typically need to design the architecture, and write the code in a modular and maintainable way, with minimal intrusions to existing code. Add new tests if the project already has tests.
- For a code refactoring, you typically need to update all the places that call the code you are refactoring if the interface changes. DO NOT change any existing logic especially in tests, focus only on fixing any errors caused by the interface changes.
- Make MINIMAL changes to achieve the goal. This is very important to your performance.
- Follow the coding style of existing code in the project.
- For broader codebase exploration and deep research, use the `Agent` tool with `subagent_type="explore"`. This is a fast, read-only agent specialized for searching and understanding codebases. Use it when your task will clearly require more than 3 search queries, or when you need to investigate multiple files and patterns. You can launch multiple explore agents concurrently to investigate independent questions in parallel.

DO NOT run `git commit`, `git push`, `git reset`, `git rebase` and/or do any other git mutations unless explicitly asked to do so. Ask for confirmation each time when you need to do git mutations, even if the user has confirmed in earlier conversations.

# General Guidelines for Research and Data Processing

The user may ask you to research on certain topics, process or generate certain multimedia files. When doing such tasks, you must:

- Understand the user's requirements thoroughly, ask for clarification before you start if needed.
- Make plans before doing deep or wide research, to ensure you are always on track.
- Search on the Internet if possible, with carefully-designed search queries to improve efficiency and accuracy.
- Use proper tools or shell commands or Python packages to process or generate images, videos, PDFs, docs, spreadsheets, presentations, or other multimedia files. Detect if there are already such tools in the environment. If you have to install third-party tools/packages, you MUST ensure that they are installed in a virtual/isolated environment.
- Once you generate or edit any images, videos or other media files, try to read it again before proceed, to ensure that the content is as expected.
- Avoid installing or deleting anything to/from outside of the current working directory. If you have to do so, ask the user for confirmation.

<current_focus>
Investigating why the p7-log zenka online-check retries in a loop despite receiving TRUE "already online" replies. The `base.log.send-buffer` system (used by nshell and other child zenki) sends `v7.notify_online`, gets back `TRUE zenka 'p7-log' already online., [sid]`, yet the idle callback later returns to the notify_online branch instead of flushing queued log lines. Previous fix (commit 696725322) prevents retry-on-FALSE; current bug occurs with TRUE replies. Need to verify if the reply handler is actually reached (route lookup / cmd_id validity) or if `paused` is reset by another path after the reply.
</current_focus>

<environment>
- Protocol-7 project at `/data/projects/protocol-7`
- nshell runs as zenka `nshell` (`p7.nshell -> bin/Protocol-7`)
- Logging target configured via `buffer.zenka.log_cmd = p7-log.append`
- `<protocol-7.network.parent_route>` controls command prefixing; child zenki prepend route hops
- Event loop uses `Event->idle` for deferred send-buffer processing and `Event->var` for `lines-added` trigger
- `system.zenka.name` for nshell is `nshell` → falls into the `else` branch of send-idle-callback that uses `v7.notify_online`
</environment>

<completed_tasks>
- **Fixed tie trap in `nshell.setup_stdin_watcher`**: Original Claude code used `@ARG` (empty in inline package) and a shared lexical `$val` that broke under p7's loader. Replaced with direct `@_` and object-scoped state (`bless \$val`, `${$_[0]}`, `$$self`). Syntax verified clean. Purpose: intercept writes starting with `(0)` to the session output buffer.
</completed_tasks>

<active_issues>
- **p7-log retry loop despite TRUE replies**: The console shows alternating `zenka 'p7-log' already online., [sid]` and `wrote N bytes`, meaning `v7.notify_online` is re-issued after successful log writes. Suspects:
  1. Reply route for `notify_online` is not matched → falls through to `unknown-reply-route`/`unknown-reply-type` hooks in nshell → reply handler never runs → `paused` stays TRUE and `n.o.-asking` stays stuck.
  2. `base.log.send-buffer.reply-handler.send-reply` receives FALSE (e.g., route/command rejected) and sets `paused = TRUE`, re-triggering the online check on next idle.
  3. `base.protocol-7.command.send.local` cmd_id format or `base.route.add` storage mismatch causes reply lookup to miss.
- **Next steps**: Verify whether `base.handler.command` successfully matches the reply route for `v7.notify_online` when it comes back to the nshell session. Check if `send.local` debug warning about invalid `target_cmd_id` fires. Confirm if `base.log.send-buffer.reply-handler.notify-online` is actually executed (add debug warn) or if reply bypasses it.
</active_issues>

<file>
modules/nshell.setup_stdin_watcher

**Summary:**
Registers STDIN watcher for nshell and currently hosts a debug Tie::Scalar trap on the session output buffer to catch `(0)` writes.

**Key elements:**
- `Nshell::OutputTrap` tied to `$session->{'buffer'}->{'output'}`
- Fixed to use `@_` and per-object storage instead of broken lexical closure

**Latest version:**
```perl
my $orig_buf = \$session->{'buffer'}->{'output'};
tie $session->{'buffer'}->{'output'}, 'Nshell::OutputTrap', $orig_buf;
{
    package Nshell::OutputTrap;
    use strict;
    use warnings;
    use Tie::Scalar;
    our @ISA = qw| Tie::StdScalar |;
    sub TIESCALAR { my $class = shift; my $val = ''; bless \$val, $class }
    sub FETCH     { ${$_[0]} // '' }
    sub STORE {
        my ( $self, $new ) = @_;
        my $val = $$self // '';
        if ( length($new) > length($val) ) {
            my $added = substr( $new, length($val) );
            if ( $added =~ /^\(0\)/ ) {
                my @c = caller(1);
                warn sprintf "[OUTPUT_TRAP] (0) written by %s line %s: [%s]\n",
                    $c[3] // '?', $c[2] // '?',
                    substr($added, 0, 60) =~ s/\n/\\n/gr;
            }
        }
        $$self = $new;
    }
}
```

modules/base.log.send-buffer.send-idle-callback

**Summary:**
Idle callback that either checks if the log target zenka is online (via `v7.notify_online` or registry checks) or sends the next queued log line.

**Key elements:**
- For non-v7/cube zenki (e.g., nshell), sends `v7.notify_online` when `paused` and not already asking
- Sends actual log command (`p7-log.append`) when `paused` is FALSE and queue has data
- Derives `route_prefix` from `<protocol-7.network.parent_route>`

**Latest version:**
```perl
my $name = length ref $ARG[0] ? shift->w->data : shift;
my $route_prefix = '';
if ( ref(<protocol-7.network.parent_route>) eq qw| ARRAY |
    and <protocol-7.network.parent_route>->@* ) {
    $route_prefix = join( '.', <protocol-7.network.parent_route>->@* ) . '.';
}
# ...
my $b_ref = <log.send-buffer>->{$name};
( my $target_zenka = $log_send_cmd ) =~ s|\..+$||;

if ( $b_ref->{'paused'} and not $b_ref->{'n.o.-asking'} ) {
    if ( <system.zenka.name> eq qw| v7 | ) {
        <v7.status-request.log-target-zenka>->{$target_zenka} = TRUE
            if $b_ref->{'paused'};
    } elsif ( <system.zenka.name> eq qw| cube | ) {
        $b_ref->{'paused'} = TRUE;
        if ( ( my $session_id ) = keys $data{'user'}{$target_zenka}->%* ) {
            $b_ref->{'paused'} = FALSE
                if $data{'session'}->{$session_id}->{'initialized'};
        }
        <cube.status-request.log-target-zenka>->{$target_zenka} = TRUE
            if $b_ref->{'paused'};
    } else {    ## other zenki using 'v7.notify_online' command ##
        <[protocol-7.command.send.local]>->(
            {   qw| command | => join( '', $route_prefix, qw| v7.notify_online | ),
                qw| call_args | => { qw| args | => $target_zenka },
                qw| reply |     => {
                    qw| handler | => qw| base.log.send-buffer.reply-handler.notify-online |,
                    qw| params | => { qw| name | => $name }
                }
            }
        );
    }
    $b_ref->{'n.o.-asking'} = TRUE;
} elsif ( $b_ref->{'data'}->$#* != -1 and defined $b_ref->{'data'}->[0] ) {
    ## target zenka online : sending log request ##
    my $line_sref = $b_ref->{'data'}->[0];
    if (    ref $line_sref eq qw| SCALAR |
        and defined $line_sref->$*
        and index( $line_sref->$*, "\n" ) > 0 ) {
        # ... error handling ...
        shift $b_ref->{'data'}->@*;
    }
    my @send_line;
    if ( <system.zenka.name> eq qw| cube | ) {
        push @send_line, join( qw| . |, <system.node.name>, <system.zenka.name> ), 0;
    }
    if ( ref $line_sref eq qw| SCALAR | and defined $line_sref->$* ) {
        push @send_line, $name, $line_sref->$*;
        <[protocol-7.command.send.local]>->(
            {   qw| command | => join( '', $route_prefix, $log_send_cmd ),
                'call_args'   => { qw| args | => join ' ', @send_line },
                qw| reply | => {
                    'handler' => qw| base.log.send-buffer.reply-handler.send-reply |,
                    qw| params | => { qw| name | => $name }
                }
            }
        );
        $b_ref->{'waiting'} = TRUE;
    }
}
```

modules/base.log.send-buffer.reply-handler.notify-online

**Summary:**
Handles the reply to `v7.notify_online`. Sets `paused = FALSE` on TRUE, keeps `paused = TRUE` on FALSE, and resets `n.o.-asking`.

**Key elements:**
- Only calls `idle-callback-set` on TRUE reply (post-commit 696725322 fix)
- On non-TRUE, stays paused and does NOT reschedule, preventing immediate loops

**Latest version:**
```perl
my $reply = shift;
my $name  = $reply->{'params'}->{'name'};

if (not <[base.is_defined_recursive]>->( sprintf qw| log.send-buffer.%s |, $name )) {
    <[base.s_warn]>->( "send-buffer '%s' no longer exists <{C1}>", $name );
    return undef;
}
my $b_ref = <log.send-buffer>->{$name};
$b_ref->{'n.o.-asking'} = FALSE;

if ( $reply->{'cmd'} eq qw| TRUE | ) {
    $b_ref->{'paused'} = FALSE;
    <[base.log.send-buffer.idle-callback-set]>->($name);
} else {
    ## target offline - stay paused, don't retry immediately
    $b_ref->{'paused'} = TRUE;
}
```
</file>

modules/base.log.send-buffer.reply-handler.send-reply

**Summary:**
Handles the reply to the actual `p7-log.append` log send. Removes line from queue on success; pauses and reschedules on failure.

**Key elements:**
- TRUE: shift queue, increment sent-lines, schedule next if more data, clear `warned-reply`
- FALSE (or error): set `paused = TRUE`, schedule idle callback to retry later

**Latest version:**
```perl
my $reply = shift;
my $name  = $reply->{'params'}->{'name'};
my $b_ref = <log.send-buffer>->{$name};

if ( $reply->{'cmd'} eq qw| TRUE | ) {
    shift $b_ref->{'data'}->@*;
```

Here is what I found about nshell-specific log buffer handling in the protocol-7 codebase:

## Summary of Findings

### 1. `buffer.zenka.log_cmd` configuration
**File:** `configuration/zenki/nshell/start` (line 50)
- nshell does **NOT** explicitly clear `buffer.zenka.log_cmd`
- It is commented out: `# buffer.zenka.log_cmd = ''`
- This means nshell **inherits** the global default from `shared-params` / `configuration/logging-configuration`, which sets `buffer.zenka.log_cmd = p7-log.append`
- nshell **does** forward log buffers to `p7-log` over the network, unlike standalone zenki like `keys`, `work`, and `sourcecode` which explicitly set `buffer.zenka.log_cmd = ''` to disable remote logging

### 2. nshell's own local buffers (not network logs)
**File:** `modules/nshell.init_code`
- `buffer.terminal-history` — a 42K local ring buffer for terminal session history, initialized with a timestamped message
- `buffer.no-tty-debug` — a 24K local debug buffer (only when `-no-tty-debug` mode is enabled)
- These are **purely local** and unrelated to the `buffer.zenka.log_cmd` network logging pipeline

### 3. `parent_route` handling
- nshell does **not** set `protocol-7.network.parent_route` explicitly
- It loads `base.net.connect`, which sets `parent_route = [$cube_name]` upon successful connection
- Log messages therefore use the normal route through cube to `p7-log.append`

### 4. Cube connection — special handling
nshell is architecturally unique in how it interacts with cube:
- **Authenticates as Unix user**, not as a zenka name (`system.auth-user = <nshell.unix_user>`)
- **Transparent relay to cube:** `nshell.shell_loop` appends user input directly to `$data{'session'}{$cube_sid}{'buffer'}{'output'}` (the cube's input stream)
- **Transparent output from cube:** `nshell.hook.input_passthrough` reads from cube's `buffer{'input'}` and writes raw bytes to STDOUT without protocol parsing
- **No reply routes:** nshell sends commands without reply routes, so it registers hooks (`unknown-reply-route`, `unknown-reply-type`) to intercept replies that would otherwise be dropped

### 5. `silent_reply_ignore` — the key special log suppression
**File:** `modules/nshell.register_hooks` (line 39)
```perl
$data{'session'}{$session_id}{'silent_reply_ignore'} = TRUE;
```
This suppresses the normal log message `"[%d] %s-reply to unknown route id [%d], ignored."` in `base.handler.command`. Without this, those log entries would be forwarded through the cube session and **misrouted to `system.p7-log.append`** when the base path is `system`.

### 6. No special prefix/format handling for log buffers
- nshell does **not** modify the format of log buffer lines sent to `p7-log`
- The custom formatting in `nshell.handler.command_reply` (two-space prefixes, `:` borders) is only for the **local** `terminal-history` buffer and for immediate STDOUT display
- Network log forwarding uses the standard `base.log.send-buffer.send-idle-callback` mechanism with `protocol-7.network.parent_route`

### 7. Current dirty/debug changes (uncommitted)
**Files with uncommitted changes:**
- `modules/nshell.setup_stdin_watcher` — added an `Nshell::OutputTrap` tied to the session output buffer to catch/debug any writes prefixed with `(0)`
- `modules/nshell.shell_loop` — added debug logging to warn if the cube output buffer already contains data before appending a new command
- `modules/base.protocol-7.command.send.local` — added validation warning for invalid `target_cmd_id` formats

These dirty changes are clearly related to debugging the `(0)` prefix / first-command routing bug mentioned in the recent commit history.

Fixed.

**Root cause:** In `base.log.send-buffer.send-idle-callback`, the `<node.zenka> <instance_id>` prefix was only prepended for `cube` zenki. Standalone child zenki like `nshell` sent log lines as just `<buffer_name> <timestamp> <level> <message>` (4 fields) instead of the 6 fields `p7-log.cmd.append` expects: `<node.zenka> <instance_id> <buffer_name> <timestamp> <level> <message>`.

Because the parameter format was wrong, `p7-log.append` returned `FALSE` with "insufficent parameters". The `send-reply` handler set `paused = TRUE`, which on the next idle tick triggered another `v7.notify_online` check. Even though `v7.notify_online` replied `TRUE` (p7-log *is* online), the subsequent log send immediately failed again — creating the observed loop of "already online" replies interleaved with retry attempts.

**Fix:** Removed the `if ( <system.zenka.name> eq qw| cube | )` guard so all zenki prepend `join('.', <system.node.name>, <system.zenka.name>)` and `0` to the log parameters before sending.

```diff
-    if ( <system.zenka.name> eq qw| cube | ) {   ##  manual for cube zenka  ##
-        push @send_line,                         ##[ cube has sid 0 ]##
-            join( qw| . |, <system.node.name>, <system.zenka.name> ), 0;
-    }
+    push @send_line,    ##[ all zenki prepend node.zenka and instance-id ]##
+        join( qw| . |, <system.node.name>, <system.zenka.name> ), 0;
```

Now nshell (and any other non-cube, non-v7 zenki) will send the correct 6-field format that `p7-log.append` expects, so log writes succeed and the cascade stops.
